paras: The Del Norte jail attack was a night assault on the jail at Del Norte, Colorado, on Saturday, March 4, 1882, by about a hundred men said to be stockmen, who shot two prisoners charged with cattle stealing, Arnold Howard and Frank Young. A Denver dispatch carried nationally reported Howard killed and Young mortally wounded, and many papers headlined it as a lynching of cattle thieves. A news item two months later said instead that Howard had escaped the mob and been captured near Pueblo, leaving the outcome in doubt.

According to a special to the Denver Republican, Howard and Young were arrested on a Thursday on a charge of stealing cattle and placed in the jail at Del Norte. The dispatch added that Howard had been arrested twelve times on the same charge and "in every instance was cleared." The next day an attempt to break the jail was prevented, though versions differ on whether the prisoners tried to break out or others tried to break in.

On Saturday night a hundred men, "said to be stock men from the Rio Grande and San Luis valleys," rode down on the jail guards, ordered them to throw up their hands and began firing in every direction. Most texts describe the men as mounted, while the Washington Evening Star and other papers called them masked. When the jail was broken open the prisoners tried to escape, and in the wire account Howard was killed outright and Young mortally wounded. Howard's body was thrown into the river, and the jail windows were riddled with bullets.

No report of an inquest, of arrests of any of the attackers, or of Young's death appears in the coverage. In May a syndicated news item described "the Del Norte horse and cattle thief" Howard as having escaped from a mob that took him from jail to hang him, and reported him surprised on a ranch near Pueblo "on the 6th" and captured after a desperate resistance.

The story reached the press as a single Denver Republican special dated March 6 or 7, which papers from Sacramento and Yankton to Washington and New York printed on March 7 and 8, often word for word. Headlines named the victims as criminals: the Yankton Press and Dakotaian ran "CATTLE THIEVES LYNCHED" with the deck "Del Norte Vigilantes Make Short Work of Cattle Thieves," the Gold Hill Daily News "Determined Lynchers," and the Savannah Morning News "CATTLE THIEVES SHOT." The Tombstone Epitaph titled its version "A Colorado Matinee."

Weeklies and digests compressed the story further, sometimes into a single line. The Lancaster Intelligencer and the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic had both prisoners riddled with bullets, and the Fairfield News and Herald of South Carolina said a Colorado mob had "lynched two cattle stealers," adding that "The morals of the menagerie at the West are being maintained." No paper in the coverage gave the race of the prisoners or the attackers; the only label attached to the victims was "cattle thieves." The escape report ran in the Milan Exchange of Tennessee on May 13 and in the Patron of Husbandry on May 27.

Accounts conflict on whether Howard died: the March wire said he was killed outright and his body thrown into the river, while the May item said he escaped the mob and was later captured. The two-killed versions in the digests are condensed from the wire story, which had Young only mortally wounded. The Watertown Republican put the attack on the 7th, the date of the Denver dispatch, while the Elko Independent gave the night of the 4th, which matches the wire's "Saturday night."

bases: About a hundred armed men attacked the Del Norte jail at night, fired on the guards, broke in and shot two prisoners charged with cattle stealing, killing one according to the wire report (A3, A5, A4).

The March wire report says a body of about a hundred men broke open the jail and killed Arnold Howard outright and mortally wounded Frank Young, both held on cattle-stealing charges (A3, A5, A8); but a May news item says Howard escaped the mob and was later captured near Pueblo (A26), and no report confirming Young's death was found, so whether anyone died is unsettled.
Many papers carried the same Denver Republican special on the attack (A3, A5, A4, A8), but a later item says Howard survived and escaped the mob (A26), contradicting the report of his death.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Denver Republican special unchanged under headlines such as 'CATTLE THIEVES LYNCHED' or 'A Jail Attacked and Prisoners Shot', calling the victims cattle thieves without qualification.
The Yankton Press and Dakotaian's deck 'Del Norte Vigilantes Make Short Work of Cattle Thieves' and the Tombstone Epitaph's 'A Colorado Matinee' treated the attack lightly.
The Fairfield News and Herald's gossip column remarked sarcastically that 'The morals of the menagerie at the West are being maintained.'
